title: Lawrence of Arabia (film)
wiki_lead:
Lawrence of Arabia is a 1962 epic biographical drama film directed by David Lean and produced by Sam Spiegel through the latter's British company Horizon Pictures and distributed by Columbia Pictures. It is based on the life of T. E. Lawrence and his 1926 book Seven Pillars of Wisdom (also known as Revolt in the Desert). Lawrence of Arabia introduces Peter O'Toole as Lawrence, with Alec Guinness playing Prince Faisal. It also stars Jack Hawkins, Anthony Quinn, Omar Sharif, Anthony Quayle, Claude Rains, Jose Ferrer and Arthur Kennedy. The screenplay was written by Robert Bolt and Michael Wilson.
Lawrence of Arabia depicts Lawrence's experiences in the Ottoman provinces of Hejaz and Syria during the First World War, in particular his attacks on Aqaba and Damascus and his involvement in the Arab National Council. Its themes include Lawrence's emotional struggles with the violence inherent in war, his identity, and his divided allegiance between Britain and his new-found comrades within the Arabian desert tribes.
In 1963, Lawrence of Arabia was nominated for ten Oscars at the 35th Academy Awards, winning seven, including Best Picture and Best Director. It also won the Golden Globe Award for Best Motion Picture – Drama and the BAFTA Awards for Best Film and Outstanding British Film. The dramatic score by Maurice Jarre and the Super Panavision 70 cinematography by Freddie Young also won praise from critics.
Lawrence of Arabia is widely regarded as one of the greatest films ever made. In 1991, it was deemed "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant" by the United States Library of Congress and selected for preservation in the National Film Registry. Although primarily a British production, it was eligible due to Columbia Pictures involvement in financing and making the production, as well as helping get the film released. In 1998, the American Film Institute placed Lawrence of Arabia fifth on their list of the greatest American films; in 2007, they placed it seventh on an updated list. The British Film Institute named Lawrence of Arabia the third-greatest British film in 1999. In 2004, it was voted the best British film in The Sunday Telegraph's poll of Britain's leading filmmakers.

Plot
T. E. Lawrence dies in a motorcycle accident in 1935. At a memorial service at St Paul's Cathedral, it becomes clear that several influential Britons disliked him.
During the First World War, Lawrence is a misfit British Army lieutenant, notable for his effrontery and education. Mr. Dryden of the Arab Bureau sends him to meet with Colonel Harry Brighton, who advises Prince Feisal in his revolt against the Turks. Lawrence is outraged when his guide is killed by Sherif Ali ibn el Kharish for drinking from the latter's well. Lawrence accuses Ali of being a barbarian and is dismayed to learn that the latter is Feisal's advisor.
Relations between the British and the Arabs are tense. While the British will supply guns to the Arabs, they will not provide artillery, which would make Feisal an independent force. Feisal is impressed by Lawrence's familiarity with the Quran and his honesty about British interests in Arabia.
Lawrence violates Brighton's orders by convincing Feisal to launch a surprise attack on Aqaba to improve his supply lines. Ali protests, as Aqaba is protected from land attacks by the Nefud Desert and the local Turkish enforcer, Howeitat tribal leader Auda Abu Tayi. Feisal gives Lawrence just fifty men. Lawrence hires teenage orphans Daud and Farraj as his attendants.
During the march to Aqaba, Lawrence wins over Feisal's men by returning to the desert to rescue Gasim. The grateful Arabs give Lawrence traditional clothing. Lawrence convinces Auda to switch sides by promising him a Turkish gold hoard at Aqaba. En route, Lawrence is shaken when he must execute Gasim to prevent a conflict between Feisal's men and Auda's.

grok_lead: Lawrence of Arabia is a 1962 epic biographical adventure-drama film directed by David Lean, chronicling the wartime exploits of British archaeologist and officer T. E. Lawrence in fomenting and leading the Arab Revolt against Ottoman rule during the First World War. Starring Peter O'Toole in his breakthrough role as Lawrence, alongside Alec Guinness, Anthony Quinn, Jack Hawkins, Omar Sharif, and JosÃ© Ferrer, the film adapts elements from Lawrence's memoir Seven Pillars of Wisdom into a sweeping narrative of guerrilla warfare, personal transformation, and imperial intrigue across the Arabian Peninsula. Produced by Sam Spiegel with groundbreaking 70mm Super Panavision cinematography by Freddie Young and an original score by Maurice Jarre, it emphasizes vast desert landscapes and logistical challenges of filming on location in Jordan, Spain, and Morocco. The production spanned over two years, involving thousands of extras and Bedouin tribesmen, and originally ran 222 minutes before cuts for release, showcasing Lean's mastery of epic scale and visual storytelling that prioritized spectacle over strict chronology. Critically lauded for its technical achievements, the film secured seven Academy Awards at the 35th ceremony, including Best Picture, Best Director for Lean, Best Cinematography, and Best Original Score, while grossing over $70 million worldwide against a $15 million budget, cementing its status as a landmark in cinema history. Notable controversies surround its dramatizations, including an amplified portrayal of Lawrence's battlefield heroismâsuch as the exaggerated Aqaba raidâand a romanticized depiction of Arab unity under his influence, diverging from historical records where tribal alliances were more fractious and Lawrence's advisory role less singularly decisive. The film faced bans and censorship in Arab countries like Jordan for perceived slights to Ottoman heritage and depictions of violence, including implied sexual assault, reflecting tensions over its Western lens on colonial-era events. Despite such liberties, it endures for authentically capturing the harsh causality of desert warfare and Lawrence's documented charisma in rallying disparate forces, though modern analyses highlight how Lean's vision privileges individual agency over broader geopolitical machinations.
